strengths: Clear and well-motivated contribution: ProstaTD addresses genuine, well-articulated limitations of CholecT50 (no bounding boxes, inconsistent temporal boundaries, single-source data), and Table 1 convincingly positions the dataset relative to prior work.

Substantial annotation effort: 165,567 triplet instances with precise bounding boxes across 21 videos from three heterogeneous sources, produced via a rigorous multi-phase, multi-annotator protocol (48 annotators, iterative semi-automatic refinement, expert adjudication) — the largest fully-supervised surgical triplet detection dataset to date.

Clinically grounded temporal boundary definition (continuous vs. momentary actions with explicit contact-based rules) is a novel and meaningful methodological contribution that reduces annotation ambiguity, and the annotation guidelines/tools (LabelTri) are promised for release.

The proposed Triplet tracking perspective (track IDs tied to instrument-action-target composition) is a thoughtful extension of existing tracking taxonomies and adds value beyond detection annotations.

Comprehensive benchmarking: the evaluation covers weakly supervised adaptations (Tripnet-Det, RDV-Det), DETR- and YOLO-based detectors, and a new YOLO-Triplet baseline, quantifying the large gap between weak and full supervision, plus precision/recall analysis and complexity comparisons with CholecT50.
Appropriate treatment of ethics, licensing (CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0), patient privacy, and broader impact including misuse mitigation.
weaknesses: Limited evidence of annotation quality: despite multiple review rounds, no quantitative inter-annotator agreement, consistency scores, or agreement statistics are reported in the main paper, making it hard to assess label reliability — critical for a dataset paper whose central claim is annotation quality.

Evaluation scope is narrow: only 5 test videos and 2 validation videos; results lack variance estimates, statistical significance, or cross-validation, so conclusions about method ranking (e.g., YOLOv10 vs. YOLO-Triplet) rest on a very small test set.

The proposed YOLO-Triplet baseline is unconvincing: it achieves the best mAP_I but underperforms YOLOv10 on action/target mAP, and its F1 gain (31.26 vs. 31.13) is marginal; the methodological novelty of the baseline is limited and the ablation of its components is deferred entirely to supplementary material.

The 'multi-institutional' claim is somewhat overstated: 9 of 21 videos come from a single in-house source, and the paper leaves institution names blank (appearing as gaps in text and figures), which weakens transparency for a final resource; released dataset details should be complete.

Presentation issues undermine polish: typos ('EASD' vs. 'ESAD', 'Surigcal', 'Comparision'), first-person phrasing in Section 6.1 ('Below, I will analyze'), duplicated figure panel captions in Fig. 4, missing dataset/GitHub URL in the abstract, and inconsistent citation of reference [18]/[22] (same paper cited twice with different numbers).

Several important analyses (confusion matrices, dataset partition statistics, tracking baselines, full YOLO-Triplet architecture) are deferred to supplementary material, making the main paper's evaluation section feel incomplete.
No discussion of computational cost of reproducing the benchmark or of standardized evaluation code for future submissions, which affects reproducibility as a benchmark.

strengths: The dataset addresses a genuine gap: existing surgical triplet datasets (e.g., CholecT50) lack bounding-box annotations and clinically grounded temporal boundaries, and ProstaTD provides dense, fully supervised annotations with multi-source data (21 videos, 165K instances), which is a useful resource for the surgical data science community.

The annotation protocol is described in reasonable detail, including clinically informed definitions of continuous vs. momentary action boundaries, a semi-automatic instrument annotation pipeline with iterative model fine-tuning, and multi-round expert review.

A reasonably broad set of baselines is evaluated (weakly supervised adaptations, DETR-based and YOLO-based detectors, and a new two-stage YOLO-Triplet baseline), and the paper is transparent that absolute performance remains far from clinical deployment.
The introduction of a 'Triplet Perspective' for tracking annotations and the analysis of concurrency/complexity relative to CholecT50 provide some novel dataset-design discussion.
weaknesses: Severe anonymization/presentation failures: institution names are left blank or missing in multiple places (Fig. 1 caption, Sec. 3.2, Sec. 5.1, Fig. 2, and the Ethical Statement 'approved by the IRB of ___'). This makes the double-blind compliance status unclear, prevents verification of IRB approval and data provenance, and signals a careless submission.

The core novelty claim is overstated. The dataset is substantially built on two existing public datasets (8 PSI-AVA and 4 ESAD videos re-annotated); only 9 videos are newly collected. The 'largest and most diverse' claim rests on a marginal instance count difference over CholecT50 (165,567 vs. 161,988) with far fewer videos (21), and Table 1 comparisons are framed to favor the proposed dataset.

Evaluation is weak for a dataset paper. The test set contains only 5 randomly selected videos with no fixed public protocol, no repeated runs or variance reporting, no statistical significance tests, and the metric definition (detection mAP 'directly computed based on the component categories') is vague and inconsistent with prior work, making results hard to interpret or reproduce.

Results are underwhelming and not clearly analyzed: best triplet-level mAP is ~36% at IoU 0.5 and F1 ~31%; the proposed YOLO-Triplet only marginally improves F1 (31.26 vs. 31.13) over its own YOLOv12 backbone, and the paper itself concedes the relation-modeling head is limited. The claimed benefit of fine-grained spatial supervision is not demonstrated via targeted comparisons (e.g., same model trained with/without boxes).

Section 6 (tracking) promises baseline experiments and detailed analysis but defers everything to supplementary materials; the main paper contains only descriptive statistics, and Figure 4 has labeling errors (both subfigures captioned as 'Intraoperative Track Distribution').

Numerous editorial defects undermine confidence: inconsistent naming ('ESAD' vs. 'EASD'), typos ('Surigcal', 'Comparision'), garbled figure labels (e.g., '1a.00', '8 68'), and an incomplete reference [5] ('Armine ... Gonzalez').

Licensing and redistribution compliance for the re-annotated PSI-AVA and ESAD portions is asserted only briefly; the justification for discarding existing annotations and re-annotating is thin given the added cost, and dataset-scale claims (frames, instances) are not normalized per video to support the 'largest' claim fairly.

Several important details needed for reproducibility are deferred to supplementary materials (split statistics, model details, annotation protocols), and the promised GitHub release is only vaguely referenced ('available at Github' without a link).

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and well-motivated gap: existing surgical triplet datasets (CholecT50) lack bounding box annotations, clinically grounded temporal boundaries, and source diversity. ProstaTD is, to my knowledge, the first dataset to provide dense frame-level bounding box annotations of full instrument-action-target triplets in a procedure beyond cholecystectomy, which is a clear contribution.

The annotation effort is substantial and well documented: 165,567 instances over 60,529 frames from 21 videos across three heterogeneous sources, with 50+ annotators, iterative semi-automatic bounding box labeling, multi-round expert review, and clear annotation protocols (continuous vs. momentary actions, bbox conventions, category merging rules). The two custom annotation tools (modified LabelMe, LabelTri) being released is a plus.

The complexity analysis (Tables 2 and 7) quantitatively demonstrates that prostatectomy scenes are substantially more challenging than cholecystectomy (much higher instrument concurrency and per-frame triplet density), which credibly motivates the dataset rather than merely asserting it.

A broad and reasonable evaluation suite is provided: weakly supervised adaptations (Tripnet-Det, RDV-Det) versus fully supervised detectors (DETR- and YOLO-family), plus a purpose-built YOLO-Triplet baseline, with mAP at IoU 50/50:95, per-component metrics, P/R/F1, and FPS. Honest discussion of the low absolute performance and remaining headroom strengthens credibility.

The tracking extension (Intraoperative and newly proposed Triplet perspectives, 204/953 track IDs) and the limitations, broader impact, and ethics sections are thoughtful, including license (CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0) and risk mitigation discussion.
The paper is transparent that existing public annotations from ESAD/PSI-AVA were not reused and everything was re-annotated under a unified protocol, which avoids inconsistent-label confounds.
weaknesses: The core novelty is partly overstated: 12 of the 21 videos are existing public datasets (ESAD, PSI-AVA) re-annotated, so the genuinely new data is 9 in-house videos. The 'first large-scale, multi-source' framing leans heavily on re-annotation effort, and the instance-count gain over CholecT50 (165,567 vs. 161,988) is marginal. Table 1's comparison, while useful, is constructed to favor the proposed dataset.

Writing quality and polish are below the bar for a top venue: multiple incomplete sentences where institution names appear to have been removed ('collected from the .', 'our in-house collection at ,' 'IRB of .'), inconsistent dataset naming ('ESAD' vs. 'EASD' in Fig. 2/Fig. 1), and typos ('Surigcal', 'Comparision'). Some of this likely stems from anonymization, but the resulting text is broken and should be rewritten (e.g., 'a hospital whose identity is withheld for double-blind review').

The evaluation is thin for generalization claims: only 21 videos total, a 5-video test set, and no repeated runs, variance estimates, or statistical significance tests. Given the paper's emphasis on multi-source diversity, a cross-source evaluation (e.g., train on one source, test on another) demonstrating actual generalization benefit would be far more convincing than the current random split; none is reported.

The proposed YOLO-Triplet baseline is only modestly better than the strongest off-the-shelf detector (mAP_IVT 50: 36.02 vs. 35.05 for YOLOv10), and it is worse on the verb and target branches. The paper frames this as evidence of open research problems, but the methodological contribution of the paper is thus limited to the dataset itself; the baseline adds little beyond completeness. Key architectural details are deferred to supplementary material, which I could not assess.

Several important quality-control details are missing: no inter-annotator agreement statistics (e.g., kappa) for the triplet/action/target labels, no reported bbox annotation accuracy or validation protocol numbers, and no analysis of how annotation noise affects the reported mAP. For a paper whose central claim is annotation quality, this is a notable omission.

Some claims are not fully supported: the assertion that ESAD is a robot-assisted prostatectomy dataset may be inaccurate (ESAD is commonly described as containing laparoscopic cholecystectomy and robot-assisted partial nephrectomy videos), which would affect both Table 1 and the dataset characterization. This should be verified and clarified. Similarly, the mAP computation 'differs from the classification task' but the exact detection-mAP protocol (matching rules, per-triplet-class AP) is underspecified in the main text.

The Section 6 discussion of tracking perspectives contains subjective, argumentative claims (e.g., that the Intracorporeal perspective 'holds limited clinical significance') that read as positioning against CholecTrack20 rather than neutral analysis, and the tracking experiments themselves are deferred entirely to supplementary material, leaving Section 6 mostly descriptive.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated contribution: the paper convincingly identifies the key gaps in existing surgical triplet resources (no bounding boxes, ambiguous temporal boundaries, single-institution data) and introduces the first fully supervised, multi-institutional surgical triplet detection dataset (ProstaTD) with 71,775 frames, 196,490 instances, 89 triplet classes, and clinically defined temporal boundaries.

Rigorous and transparent annotation methodology: a unified annotation protocol, semi-automatic instrument labeling with five iterative refinement cycles, multi-phase medical expert review, documented label consolidation rules (Appendix A.4), and an inter-rater agreement study (average Cohen's Kappa 0.82 with independent surgeons) support annotation quality claims.

Strong community resource value: two purpose-built open-source annotation tools (Triplet-labelme, SurgLabel) and an enhanced evaluation toolkit (ivtdmetrics) with COCO-style global ranking, video-wise mAP, and P/R/F1 evaluation address real workflow gaps in this sub-field.

Comprehensive benchmarking: 12+ methods including weakly-supervised challenge baselines, classical detectors, SOTA detectors (RT-DETR, YOLOv10-12), and task-specific methods (TAPIR, MCIT-IG), all under a documented 5-fold cross-validation protocol with released splits, plus a tailored TDnet baseline with ablations (Table 9), video-wise results, confusion matrix, and per-class AP analysis.

Thorough dataset analysis: complexity comparison with CholecT50 (Table 2), component/triplet distributions (Fig. 3, Table 6), cross-source diversity analysis, and an honest treatment of long-tail limitations (Appendix G).

Good reproducibility and ethics practices: anonymous repository with data, tools, toolkit, and training scripts; IRB approval, anonymization, licensing, and a societal impact discussion with mitigation measures.
weaknesses: Scale is moderate in terms of source diversity: only 21 videos, of which 12 come from two existing public datasets (ESAD, PSI-AVA) and only 9 are newly collected; claims of 'largest and most diverse' rest largely on re-annotating public data. The 71,775-frame count also implies heavy subsampling (likely ~1 fps), which limits fine temporal granularity and may hamper temporal modeling, as acknowledged in Appendix G.2.

The inter-rater agreement study is relatively small: five 200-frame segments (1,000 frames total out of 71,775), with each surgeon reviewing only one segment; agreement was also measured against the consolidated ground truth rather than between annotators, which may inflate Kappa.
Temporal boundary rules (e.g., the 2-second departure/momentary-action windows) are pragmatic but somewhat ad hoc; sensitivity of model performance to these choices is not analyzed.

The proposed TDnet's advantage over the best baseline (YOLOv12) is modest (36.1% vs 34.3% mAP_IVT@0.5), and per-class results (Table 10) show several regressions (e.g., scissors,coagulate,prostate drops to 0.0; forceps,suture,bladder from 26.8 to 8.8), so the method contribution is secondary and should not be oversold.

Domain coverage is restricted to robot-assisted prostatectomy (single procedure type); cross-procedure or cross-domain generalization (e.g., to cholecystectomy) is not evaluated, which weakens the claimed generalizability benefit of multi-source data.

Some positioning claims (e.g., 'first open-source annotation tool purpose-built for surgical triplets', 'first fully supervised triplet detection benchmark') are difficult to verify exhaustively, and the CholecQ comparison, while argued, is somewhat dismissive.
Minor presentation issues: hyperlinks/URLs are placeholders or missing in the abstract and reproducibility statement; the abstract's final sentence is incomplete ('available at .').

strengths: Introduces the first fully-supervised, instance-annotated dataset for surgical triplet detection, moving the field beyond frame-level weak supervision in CholecT50

Substantial annotation effort with a rigorous protocol: multi-phase labeling by 60+ annotators, expert-defined temporal boundary rules, and an inter-rater agreement study (Cohen's Kappa 0.82) — uncommonly thorough for surgical datasets
Multi-institutional, multi-source composition (PWH, ESAD, PSI-AVA) with documented distribution differences across sources, supporting generalization claims

Releases reusable infrastructure: two purpose-built annotation tools (Triplet-labelme, SurgLabel) and an improved evaluation toolkit (ivtdmetrics) with COCO-style mAP, video-wise metrics, and bug fixes over prior ivtmetrics

Comprehensive benchmarking: 12+ baselines spanning classical and modern detectors, 5-fold cross-validation with published splits, ablations, confusion matrix, and per-class AP analysis; includes weakly-supervised baselines to quantify the supervision gap
Ethical statement, IRB approval, anonymization, licensing, and reproducibility statement are all present
weaknesses: Limited truly new data: 12 of 21 videos are re-annotations of existing public datasets (ESAD, PSI-AVA); the core contribution is largely a re-labeling effort rather than new clinical data, weakening novelty claims of a 'new dataset'

Scale and scope are modest for 'largest and most diverse' claims: only 21 videos from a single procedure type (RARP), ~72k frames, and a single-camera domain; cross-procedure generalization remains untested

The proposed TDnet improvement is marginal and possibly not statistically meaningful: +1.8 mAP IVT@0.5 over YOLOv12 with reported stds of ±3.4, making the headline method gain within noise; the 'Ours' framing overstates significance

Severe class imbalance and heavy use of 'null' actions/targets (e.g., scissors,null,null at 19,651 instances) raises questions about whether the annotation scheme reflects clinically meaningful triplet activity or dilutes the task
Only 1 of 21 videos is validated per inter-rater segment (5×200 frames), a small sample for claims about annotation consistency across 71,775 frames

Dataset availability is promised ('will be released', CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0) rather than demonstrably verified at review time; licensing statements ('reserve the right to take legal action') are in tension with the stated license terms

Label consolidation (merging of triplets in Appendix A.4) appears somewhat ad hoc and under-justified clinically; the mapping from raw labels to the 89 final classes could materially affect benchmark conclusions
The temporal boundary protocol (2-second rules) is novel but validated only through the limited agreement study; its impact on temporal modeling and downstream metrics is not analyzed

Fit for a top-tier general AI venue is questionable: the technical novelty (a YOLO-based detector with self-distillation) is incremental, and the contribution is primarily of interest to a specialized surgical data science community

strengths: Significant resource contribution: ProstaTD is, to the authors' convincing justification, the largest and most diverse fully-supervised surgical triplet detection dataset (71,775 frames, 196,490 instances, 21 videos from three heterogeneous sources), addressing a genuine gap—existing benchmarks (CholecT45/50) provide only weak frame-level labels without bounding boxes.

Careful and transparent annotation methodology: clinically informed temporal boundary definitions (continuous vs. momentary vs. null actions), unified bounding box rules, expert-guided label consolidation with documented merge rules (Appendix A.4), and a rigorous multi-stage quality-control process involving surgeons and medically trained annotators.

Strong annotation quality validation: inter-rater agreement study with five independent surgeons yielding Cohen's Kappa of 0.82, with a consensus resolution protocol; this goes beyond what many dataset papers provide.

Comprehensive ecosystem: two purpose-built open-source annotation tools (Triplet-labelme, SurgLabel), an enhanced evaluation toolkit (ivtdmetrics) with clearly documented improvements over ivtmetrics, COCO/YOLO dual formats, and a fixed five-fold cross-validation protocol enabling reproducible benchmarking.

Thorough benchmarking: 14 methods spanning classical detectors, modern YOLO/DETR variants, weakly-supervised challenge methods, and surgical-specific approaches (TAPIR, MCIT-IG), evaluated under both global and video-wise protocols, with ablation, per-class AP, and confusion matrix analyses that give clear insight into remaining challenges (long-tail, verb/target confusion).

Well-written paper with a clear problem motivation (three concrete CholecT50 limitations), a detailed dataset complexity analysis (higher instrument concurrency vs. CholecT50), and complete reproducibility and ethical statements.
weaknesses: The tailored baseline TDnet's margin over the strongest baseline (YOLOv12) is modest (e.g., 36.1% vs. 34.3% mAPIVT@0.5, with overlapping standard deviations), so its claimed advantage is suggestive rather than definitive; the self-distillation design rationale, while sensible, is incremental.

Overall mAPIVT remains low (~33–34%), partly reflecting heavy class imbalance; while the authors acknowledge this honestly, it leaves open questions about whether the annotation granularity (89 triplet classes) is the most useful formulation versus compositional prediction of instruments/verbs/targets separately.

All data is from RARP only; despite claims of enabling generalization across procedures, there are no cross-domain or cross-procedure transfer experiments to support the generality claims, and the diversity argument rests mainly on three heterogeneous sources of the same procedure type.

Dataset scale, while the largest of its kind, is still modest in absolute terms (21 videos), and temporal modeling aspects (triplet boundaries) are not exercised by the benchmark, since all baselines are frame-level detectors; a video-level (temporal action detection) baseline would strengthen the temporal-boundary contribution.

Some evaluation details raise minor concerns: the F1 threshold is selected by maximizing global F1 (which favors methods tuned to that criterion), and variance in Table 5 is relatively large for several methods.
